WEEKLY PRODUCTION MIX OPTIMIZER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

What should you make this week?

List what you make, what each product earns and how much of each limited resource (oven hours, labour, machine time) it uses. The optimizer finds the most profitable mix in whole batches, with your promised minimums, your demand limits and optional overtime — and shows what one more hour of your bottleneck is worth and what each product really earns once it crowds out the others.

Arithmetic on figures you supply. Not legal, tax, or financial advice. New to this? Read why your best margin product may not be your best product.

Limited resources (per week)

Anything that runs out: hours of an oven, machine or person, a shared tool, a stock of material. The order matters: product usage columns follow it.

Your products

Unit cost is materials and anything else you pay per unit. Minimum is what you have promised; maximum is the most you can sell (blank for no limit). Batch size is how many come out of one run, tray or case (1 for single units). Use per unit is in the same units as the resource, in the same order as the list on the left.

Add your resources and products, then click Find the best mix.

Resource cost per unit is each resource the product uses times what one more unit of that resource is worth. A negative net means the product earns less than the production it crowds out.

How it is calculated

Model: maximise the sum of margin (price less unit cost) times units, less overtime cost, subject to each resource's capacity plus overtime, each product's minimum and maximum, and whole batches. The linear program is solved with a two-phase simplex method (Bland's rule, which cannot cycle), and whole batches are found by branch and bound; the page says whether that search finished or stopped at its limit. One more unit is worth: the shadow price, read by re-solving with a little more of that resource, together with how much more it holds for before the plan changes shape; it is a continuous figure for the next unit, not a promise for a whole shift. Resource cost per unit: the resource use times those prices. Rules of thumb: two greedy plans — best margin per unit first, and best margin per unit of your tightest resource first — filled up to your maximums without overtime.

Not modelled: setup or changeover time and cost, minimum run sizes beyond your batch size, ingredients shared between products unless you list them as a resource, shelf life, sequencing within a week, demand that falls as you sell more, taxes and overheads other than the fixed cost you enter, and costs or usage that change with volume. Usage and costs are assumed constant per unit. Unverified against a real business's books: tests use hand-solved problems, brute-force comparison and duality checks.

Common questions

How do I decide what to make when I cannot make everything?

Compare products by what they earn per unit of the thing that runs out, not per unit sold. A product with a large margin that takes most of a scarce oven hour can earn less than a small one that takes a tenth of it. List your resources, the hours or units each product uses, your minimums and your demand limits, and the optimizer finds the combination with the most profit.

What is a shadow price, and why does it matter to a small business?

It is what one more unit of a limited resource would add to profit while the plan stays the same shape: the value of one more oven hour, one more hour of labour, one more machine day. Compare it with what extra capacity costs you (overtime, a second shift, hiring) to see whether buying it pays. The tool also shows how many extra units that value holds for.

Why does the tool charge each product for the resources it uses?

Because a unit margin ignores what the product displaces. The resource cost per unit is the resource use multiplied by the shadow prices; the net per unit is the margin minus that. A product with a negative net is costing you more in crowded-out production than it earns, which is why it is left out of the plan.

Can it handle batch sizes, minimum orders and overtime?

Yes. Give each product a batch size (trays, runs, cases) and it plans in whole batches. Give each a minimum for orders you have promised and a maximum for demand you can really sell. For each resource you can enter overtime hours available and what each costs; overtime is used only where it pays.

Is the answer guaranteed to be the best plan?

For the figures you enter, when the batch search finishes it is the best whole-batch plan, and the page says so. If a very large problem reaches the search limit the page reports how close the plan is to the theoretical upper bound. The result is only as good as your usage figures and costs, which are assumed to be constant per unit.

Is my data uploaded?

No. The optimizer runs in your browser from the figures you type, nothing is sent to a server, there are no accounts, and it works offline after the page loads.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice and does not replace your accountant or a production planner. Results are arithmetic on the figures you type; prices, costs and capacities change and every one of them is yours to check. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before acting on it.

Independent. Not affiliated with any bakery supplier, equipment maker, planning software or marketplace, and none is named or ranked here. The example products, prices and hours are invented.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you enter, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere.

Everything runs in your browser. Your figures are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (plan_run, example_loaded, report_downloaded) are counted only in local storage on your device, never with any of your data, and are switched off by Do Not Track.

Related tools: the restaurant menu mix analyzer, the dog grooming profit calculator, the appointment overbooking optimizer and the seasonal buy quantity optimizer. and, for a household rather than a business, the cheapest meal plan optimizer, the same cost-minimising linear program

Why your best margin product may not be your best product

When you can sell more than you can make, something is the limit: oven hours, a machine, a person, a bench. Every product draws on that limit at a different rate, so the product that earns the most per unit is often not the one that earns the most per hour of the thing that runs out. The way to see it is to price the limit, then charge each product for the share of it that it uses.

Open the free production mix optimizer

A worked example

An invented bakery has 40 oven hours a week. A custom cake sells for $50, costs $10 in materials and takes 4 oven hours: a $40 margin. A bun sells for $5, costs $1 and takes 0.2 hours: a $4 margin. The bakery can sell up to 10 cakes and 1,000 buns a week.

PlanCakesBunsWeekly margin
Highest margin per unit first100$400
Optimizer0200$800

Ten cakes use all 40 hours and earn $400, or $10 an hour. Two hundred buns use the same 40 hours and earn $800, or $20 an hour. The optimizer prices an oven hour at $20: that is the shadow price, what one more hour would add while the plan keeps its shape. It holds for another 160 hours, because after that the bun demand limit of 1,000 is reached. Charging each product for the oven hours it uses, a cake costs 4 × $20 = $80 of crowded-out production against a $40 margin, so its net per unit is −$40, while a bun's net is $0: it is exactly the break-even product at the margin.

None of those figures is real; the method is what matters. Notice what the answer does not say: it does not say cakes are bad. If a customer wants a cake at $90, the margin is $80 and the net is zero, and the plan would change. The tool shows the price at which a product earns its place by showing its resource cost.

Finding your own gap

  1. List the things that run out in a week and how much of each you have. Add overtime you could buy and what it costs.
  2. For every product, enter its price, its per-unit cost, how much of each limit one unit uses, a batch size if you make them in trays or runs, the minimum you have promised and the most you can sell.
  3. Read the plan, then the value of one more unit of each limit, and compare that with what extra capacity costs you.
  4. Look at the net per unit of products that did not make the plan: that is how much more each would have to earn to be worth making.

Common questions

Should I always make the product with the highest margin?

Not when you cannot make everything. Margin per unit ignores how much of a scarce resource each unit consumes. Compare products by what they earn per unit of the resource that runs out; the optimizer does that for every resource at once.

What if I have several limits at once, such as oven time and labour?

Then no single ratio works, because the best mix depends on which limit binds. That is what linear programming is for: it weighs all the limits together, and its shadow prices tell you which limit is actually costing you money this week.

How do I use the value of one more hour?

Compare it with what an extra hour costs you: overtime pay, a second shift, a rented oven, a helper. If the value is higher, buy it, up to the range the tool shows. If it is lower, the limit is not worth relaxing.

Pricing a menu rather than planning production? The restaurant menu mix analyzer looks at what sells.
